Research team to Antarctica 
†*62 PROF R.B.S. VARMA: 
SHRI PYARELAL KHANDELWAL:†† 
Will the Minister of OCEAN DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a team of Indian Scientists is being sent by 
Government to Antarctica for research works: 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the subject on which the Indian Scie ntists would undertake research at 
Antarctica; and 
(d) by when the task would be completed? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A scientific 
expedition team to Antarctica is being sent annually since 1981 by the 
Government of India. So far 24 such  expeditions have been successfully 
launched. Each year the expedition is being launched in the month of 
December/January in a chartered ve ssel. The expedition team has two 
components viz; summer and winter. The summer team will carry out the 
scientific activities and will come back in the month of March next year 
leaving behind the winter team. However the winter team will stay back in 
the Indian Antarctic Station 'Maitri' for carrying out various scientific 
experiments and will come back to the main land when the next expedition

returns after replacing them. In each  expedition around 42 scientific/ 
technical personnel belonging to various scientific institutes/universities and 
13 logistic personnel drawn from Indian Army are participating. 
(c) The scientists are carrying out the research work at Antarctica in the 
fields Meteorology & Atmospheric Sc ience; Earth Science & Glaciology; 
Biology & Environmental Sciences; Human Biology & Medicine and 
Engineering & Communication. Eight permanent observations have been 
established at Maitri, which are providing continuous data on weather, 
geomagnetism, seismicity, plate movement, Very Low Frequency (VLF) 
propagation, communication, envi ronmental assessm ent and cold 
acclimatization. 
(d) The Indian Antarctic research is an ongoing programme.

SHRI KAPIL SIBAL: MR. Chairman, Sir, I think, the hon. Member has 
asked a very important question. I wish to mention that global warming is a 
real issue that the world community is confronted with and one of the things 
that we have been doing in the Antarctica—is to measure the extent of global 
warming. Countries present in Antarctica—eighteen countries have 
permanent stations—share the data amongst themselves because till 2040 the 
Antarctica Treaty has been frozen. 
And, Antarctica as a continent can only  be used for the purposes of R&D, 
and for scientific purposes. Now, on global warming, I might mention that in 
the last 50 years we have found out that in the polar regions, that

is, the South Pole and the North Pole, the temperature has increased by 4.5 
degree centigrade. That is a very seriou s issue. Whereas the mean increase of 
temperature over the last 50 years on planet earth is only 0.5 degrees, in the 
polar regions it has increased by 4.5 degrees. What does that mean? That 
means that the ice cover in the polar regions is melting and that will increase 
the flow of water into the oceans which will, in turn, submerge very many 
low-lying areas throughout the world. I think the world community is 
grappling with this issue. Several conferences have been held on global 
warming. There is also a Kyoto Protocol for the purposes of reducing carbon 
dioxide emissions. In fact, I might ju st mention that the Antarctica is a 
continent which absorbs the maximum carbon dioxide. In a way, the 
Antarctica is also a saviour of planet earth because it seeks to absorb, but it

problem that India can resolve on its own; it is a problem that the world 
community is confronted with. I think th at the leaders of the world including 
our Prime Minister have been airing these issues within the world community 
and in India. I think that we, on our part, at the Indian end, should now have a 
legal regime to ensure that there is as much reduction of carbon dioxide as 
possible without sacrificing our interests for economic development.

capital are made available by banks to registered institutions producing khadi 
and polyvastra items. The difference between the actual interest rate of the 
bank and 4 per cent is paid by the Central Government through KVIC to the 
lending bank. The Product Development Design Intervention and Packaging 
(PRODIP) Scheme aims at assisting product quality improvement, 
introduction of new designs, marketing and packaging of khadi and village 
industry products. Under this Scheme, assistance is limited to (i) Rs. 2 lakh 
per project per year or 75 per cent of the project cost, whichever is lower, in 
cases of eligible institutional entities and (ii) Rs. 1 lakh per project per year or 
75 per cent of the project cost, whiche ver is lower, in cases of eligible 
individual entrepreneurial units. 
(b) The State/Union Territory (UT)-wise details of Interest Subsidy 
Eligibility Certificates issued by the KVIC and actual availment thereof 
during the last three years are given in Statements-I, II and III (See below). 
Since implementation of the PRODIP scheme started in 2003-04 only, the 
details of funds allocated to the States/UTs for the year 2003-04 and 2004-05 
are given in Statement-IV enclosed. 
(c) and (d) In keeping with the declaration in the National Common 
Minimum Programme and the annoucemen t in the July 2004 budget speech 
of Finance Minister, a draft scheme titled the "Scheme of Fund for 
Regeneration of Traditional Industries" (SFURTI), covering traditional 
industries like coir, khadi and village in dustries, has been prepared. The draft 
Scheme, with projected commencement during 2005-06, is based on a 
"cluster approach" and has been circ ulated to the Central Ministries/ 
Departments concerned for their comments, prior to final approval.

335. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACH ARJEE: Will the Minister of 
AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES the pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is n eed of taking steps to promote agro-
based industries in the rural areas of the country, more particularly in the 
North-East Region ridden with poverty; 
(b) if so, the projects and schemes launched in the North-East region to 
provide empk)yment to unemployed youth; end 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES (SHRI 
MAHABIR PRASAD): (a) Yet, Sir. 
(b) The Government has been implementing the Rural Employment 
Generation Programme (REGP), a credit-linked subsidy programme, through 
the Khadi and Village Industries Commssion (KVIC), throughout the 
country, including the NE Region, to assist eligible applicants in setting up 
labour-intensive industries in the rural areas and small towns with population 
up to 20,000 and thus ganerate additional 
50 

[28 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
employment. Under this programme, entrepreneurs, including unemployed 
youth, can establish village industries, by availing of margin money 
assistance from the KVIC and loans fr om any public sector scheduled 
commercial bank, for projects with a maximum cost of Rs. 25 lakh. 
Besides, the Ministry of Agro an d Rural Industries has also been 
implementing the Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana (PMRY), in both rural and 
urban areas (with approximately fifty per cent of the units being in rural 
areas), for providing self-employment opportunities to educated unemployed 
youth. This too is a credit-linked subsidy scheme and is implemented through 
the District Industries Centres of the States and Union Territories, with the 
loans being provided by banks. Under the PMRY, projects costing upto Rs. 1 
lakh for business sector and upto Rs. 2 lakh in other sectors are eligible for 
assistance, with the subsidy being limited to 15 per cent of the project cost, 
subject to a ceiling of Rs. 7,500/-. This ceiling is higher at Rs. 15,000/- per 
beneficiary, in the North Eastern (NE) region. 
During the 10th Plan period (2002-03 to 2004-05), 1121 units have been 
set up in NE Region under the REGP. Similarly, 22536 units have been set 
up under the PMRY in the NE Region during the same period. 
(c) In view of the reply at (b) above, the question does not arise.

Affordable Source of Energy 
338. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether India and U.S. are moving closer on the crucial issue of 
civilian Nuclear Energy by giving  India access to Nuclear Energy 
Technology; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is proposed to set up five working groups to expedite 
the matter; 
(d) whether first meeting of this Nuclear Energy Group will be held in the 
run up to Prime Minister's U.S. visit in July, 05; and 
(e) how far U.S. and India ensure clean,  reliable, affordable sources of 
energy to keep the economies of both countries expanding? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE 
(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) and (b) Recognizing the significance of 
civilian nuclear energy for meeting growing energy demands in cleanei and 
more efficient manner, Prime Minister during his recent US visit, discussed 
with President Bush, India's plans to  develop its civilian nuclear energy 
programme. The US side, while appreci ating India's strong commitment to 
preventing Weapons of Mass Destruction (WMD) proliferation stated that as 
a responsible State with advanced nucle ar technology, Indi a should acquire 
the same benefits and advantages as other such States. President Bush 
promised to seek agreement from Congress to US laws and policies and to 
work with friends and allies, to adjust  international regimes to enable full 
civil nuclear energy cooperation and trade with India including but not 
limited to expeditious consideration of fuel supplies for safeguarded nuclear 
reactor at Tarapur. US side also pr omised to encourage its partners to 
consider India's request for its inclusion in International Thermonuclear 
Experimental Reactor (ITER) and Genera tion IV Internationa l Forum. India, 
on its part, agreed that reciprocally it would be ready to assume the same 
responsibilities and practices and acquire the same benefits and advantages as 
other leading countries with advanced nuclear technology such as the US. 
(c) Growing concerns about energy security prompted India and the US to 
announce the agreement on 14th April 2005 on a new Energy 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2005] 
dialogue with Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission as the Co-
Chairperson on the Indian side and En ergy Secretary as the Co-Chairperson 
from the US side. The first meeting of the Energy Dialogue took place on 
31st May, 2005 in Washington DC. The meeting resulted in an understanding 
to establish a Steering Committee to supervise the five Working Groups 
under the dialogue, which would be on: Civil Nuclear Energy, Oil and Gas, 
Power and Energy Efficiency, Coal and New Technologies and Renewable 
Energy. 
(d) The first meeting of the Civil Nuclear Working group is yet to take 
place. 
(e) The India-US Energy Dialogue would focus on promoting increased 
trade and investment in the energy s ector by working with the public and 
private sectors to further identify ar eas of cooperation and collaboration. 
Building upon the broad range of existing cooperation, it is hoped that this 
effort will help mobilize secure, clean, reliable and affordable sources of 
energy.

Improving the quality of coal 
342. SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that bulk of coal produced through open cast mining 
is of very low quality; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) the steps taken in this regard to improve the quality of coal by Coal 
India Ltd.? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYANA RAO): (a ) and (b) The quality of extractable coal 
reserve in our country amenable for open cast mining is in general of lower 
quality containing more than 34% ash. As such the bulk of quantity of coal 
produced from open cast mines in the country is of inferior quality. 
(c) Following steps have been undertaken by Coal India Limited to ensure 
supply of quality coal:— 
(i) Beneficiation of the coal produced by CIL through coal washeries. 
56 

[28 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) Deployment of new technology like selective mining with the use of 
surface Miners in various open cast mines. 
(iii) Adopting Controlled blasting met hods for reducing the possibility of 
admixture of coal with over burden materials, improving fragmentation 
of coal etc. 
(iv) Picking of shales/stones before crushing and screening most of the coal 
produced by CIL in the Coal Handling Plants, thereby improving the 
quality.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYANA RAO): (a) Central Electricity Authority has reported 
that as on 19.7.2005, out of the 75 thermal power stations of the country, 13

(b) The reasons for which coal stock at power house end gets depleted 
to critical level are:- 
1. Perennial unloading constraints resulting in congestion in the rail 
movement, which in turn forces Railways to impose restriction in 
movement or rakes till congestion is cleared. 
2. Delayed release of payment by power plants for coal value as well as 
railway freight often leading to regulation in movement of coal. 
3. Constraints in transport logistics coming in the way of movement of 
coal resulting in lopsided distribution of available coal amongst power 
stations.

given by Standing Linkage Committee (Short-term).

million tonnes of coal during 2005-06.

Statement 
Increase in FDI Ceiling to 74 per cent In Telecom Sector 
The Union Cabinet on 02.02.2005 approved a proposal to enhance 
composite foreign holding in Telecom Sector to 74 per cent. With this 
decision, the current FDI ceiling in the Telecom Sect or in certain services 
such as Basic, Cellular, Unified Acce ss services, National/International Long 
Distance, V-SAT, Public Mobile Radio Trunked Services (PMRTS), Global 
Mobile Personal Communications Services (GMPCS) and other value added 
services, has been increased from 49 per cent to 74 per cent. 
The total composite foreign holding including but not limited to 
investments by Foreign Institutional Investors (Flls), Non-Resident Indians 
(NRIs), Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs), American Depository 
Receipts (ADRs), Global Deposito ry Receipts (GDRs), convertible 
preference shares, proportionate foreign investment in Indian 
promoters/investment companies including their holding companies, etc., will 
not exceed 74 per cent. Thus, 74 per cent foreign investment can be made 
directly or indirectly in the operating company or through a holding company. 
Hence, the remaining 26 per cent will be owned by resident Indian citizens or 
an Indian Company (i.e. foreign direct investment does not exceed 49 per 
cent and the management is with the In dian owners). It is clarified that 
proportionate foreign component of such an Indian Company will also be 
counted towards the ceiling of 74% . The licensee 
85 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2005] 
will be required to disclose the status of such foreign holding and certify that 
the foreign investment is within the ceiling of 74% on a half yearly basis. 
While enhancing the FDI ceiling, certain conditions have been put in 
place to safeguard the national interest. The salient conditions are: 
(a) The majority directors on the Board including Chairman, Managing 
Director and CEO shall be resident Indian citizens. The Share Holder 
Agreements (SHA) shall specifically incorporate this condition and 
also envisage the conditions of adherence to Licence Agreement. 
(b) In order to ensure that at least one serious resident Indian promoter 
subscribes reasonable amount of the resident Indian shareholding, such 
resident Indian promoter shall hold at least 10 per cent equity of the 
licensee company. 
(c) Chief Technical Officer (CTO)/ Chief Finance Officer (CFO) should be 
resident Indian citizens. The Licenso r/DoT shall also be empowered to 
notify any key positions to be held by resident Indian citizens. 
(d) No traffic ( mobile and landline) from subscribers within India to 
subscribers within India shall be hauled to any place outside India. 
(e) The Company shall not transfer the following to any person/place 
outside India: 
(i) any accounting information relating to subscribers (except for 
roaming/billing) (note: it does not restrict a statutorily required 
disclosure of financial nature); 
(ii) user information (except pertaining to foreign subscribers using 
Indian Operator's network while roaming); and 
(iii) details of their infrastructure/network diagram except to telecom 
equipment suppliers/manufacturers who undertake the 
installation, commissioning etc. of the infrastructure of the 
licensee company on signing of non-disclosure agreement. 
These conditions shall also be made applicable to the companies operating 
telecom service (s) with existing FDI ceiling of 49 per cent. With the above 
dispensation, the present provisions in FDI policy for investment company 
will no longer be applicable for Telecom Sector as 
86 

[28 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
indirect foreign investment in the licensee company will also be counted 
towards sectoral cap of 74 per cent. 
In case of not adhering to licence conditions now being imposed for 
addressing security concerns, the licence (s) granted to the company shall be 
deemed as cancelled and the licenso r shall have the right encash the 
performance bank guarantees and the licensor shall not be liable for loss of 
any kind.

New visa procedure for students visiting Australia 
384. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Australian High Commission in Delhi has 
evolved a new visa procedure for students wishing to study in Australia; 
98 

[28 July, 2005]                 RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereot; and 
(c) the number of Indian students in Australia and how is this expected to 
vary in the near future? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (c) Since November 1, 2004, 
Australia has initiated a trial of an electronic lodgement service (e-Visa). The 
new visa regulations now introduce Assessment Levels or ALs (depending on 
country and sector), which determine requirements for financial ability 
(abiiity to meet tuition and living costs), English language proficiency 
conditions and other criteria set against the Assessment Level (AL) of the 
country of citizenship. Coun tries are divided into Assessment levels 1—4. in 
some cases countries have different AL ratings depending upon the 
programme level (i.e. a different ratin g for undergraduate or postgraduate). 
Higher evidentiaiy requirements have to be met for countries falling into AL 
3-4 and lower evidentiary standards for AL 1-2. The e-Visa has been initiated 
for education agents lodging student visas for Assessment Level (AL) 2—-4 
countries. 
There are currently 3 coun tries participating in the trial—India, China and 
Thailand. The trail involves 26 Indian education agencies (with 98 of their 
staff) who nave signed an agreement with  Australia to use the e-Visa system. 
So far around 1800 e-Visa applications have been lodged by these agents on 
behalf of students. Australia has provided additional training to the education 
agents in this regard and they receive regular feedback on their performance. 
When an application is e-lodged, it is processed by Australia's Adelaide 
Students Processing Centre. The staff at the Adelaide processing centre 
provides an e-mail service to ag ents in respect of any outstanding 
documentation and the visa decision. Students must still obtain a visa label 
from the Australian High Commission in Delhi before they travel. The 
Australian High Commission in Delh i also assists in managing the 
arrangements with the agents. 
As part of their access agreement to e-Visa, agents must sign a code of 
conduct and agree to terms and conditions that apply for the lodgement of the 
applications. Agents can be checked  and audited in respect of their 
applications to ensure that they do not engage in fraudulent practices. 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2005] 
The e-Visa system for AL1 countries has been operating since 2002 and 
around 90% of students from these countries use e-Visa. Australia' is 
anticipating that students from AL 2,3 and 4 countries will also embrace the e-
Visa as well. 
Around 13,300 students visas have been granted to Indian students from 1 
July 2004 to 30 June 2005, which is around 20% more than the previous year. 
A large part of this increase (3,315) has been students applying for a further 
student visa in Australia to complete a course or to start a new course, after 
completing their first course. The number  of new initial student visas granted 
to students before they leave home has increased around 4% this year. 
Australia expects that the numbers of Indian students will continue to 
increase, but probably not at the levels experienced in past years. As on 31 
March 2005, there were around 17,600 Indian students in Australia.

425 SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Integr ated Coastal and Marine Area 
Management (ICMAM) scientists carried out extensive studies after Tsunami 
havoc of December, 2004; 
(b) if so, the details therof; 
130 

[28 July, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether any scientific study or re search has been carried out to 
forecast Tsunami and the areas prone its aftermath; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) The scientists at 
Integrated Coastal Marine Areal Mana gement (ICMAM) Project Directorate 
of Department of Ocean Development (DOD) have measured the run-up 
levels (maximum land elevation up to which sea water reached) and 
inundation limits (horizontal distances from the coast upto which sea water 
reached) during the Tsunami that occu rred on 26th December, 2004. The run 
up levels are useful in determining the safe locations for human settlement 
along the coast and also to validate models used in prediction of inundation of 
sea water on the land during Tsunami that may occur in future. The run up 
levels have been measured at a few locations in Andaman, Nicobar, Great 
Nicobar, Nagapattnam and Chennai coas t. The data collected has indicated 
maximum run up levels of 7 m in Car Nicobar, 4.4.m in Nagapattnam and 
3.5m in Chennai. The inundation limits varied from 45m to 1.2 km along 
Andaman, Nicobar and Tamil Nadu coasts. 
(c) and (d) The run up data has indicated the vulnerability of low lying 
areas to tsunami waves. It has been proposed to set up a Tsunami and Storm 
Surge Early Warning System with the following components. 
* Strengthening of the existing seismologicai network to indicate in near 
real time occurrence of tsunamigenic earthquakes. 
* Installation of tsunami warning sensors close to the ocean bottom at 
appropriate locales in the Indian Ocean with real time connectivity. 
* Tide gauge and data buoys networking. 
* Modelling of the inundations scenarios for the entire coast. 
* The establishment of a centre for collection of information analysis and 
generating status advisories. 
A component of the proposed Early Warning System comprises studies 
for forecasting of tsunami waves different magnitude earthquake scenarios. 
The results obtained will indicate the areas vulnerable to tsunami waves 
depending on the source parameters.

status and time-frame fixed to operationalise it?

Third station in Antarctica 
427. SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR : Will the Minister of OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India's third station in Antarctica with the state-
of-the-art and world class facilities would be ready by 2008; 
(b) if so, the location of the third station and the details of how it proposes 
to function; and 
(c) the details of work done by the previous two stations in Antarctica? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF OCEAN 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) and (b) No, Sir. However, a 
site near latitude 69° South and longitude 76° East has been identified for 
setting up of third Indian Antarctic Station. Preliminary surveys on 
environmental parameters as mandated under the Environmental Protocol of 
the Antarctic Treaty and also from logistics and scientific considerations, 
have been carried out during the last two summer expeditions. Further studies 
and surveys are being planned to develop a detailed plan proposal for getting 
necessary clearances as per the Protocol for the new station. 
(c) The 'Dakshin Gangotri' station, which was established in the Antarctic 
summer of 1983/1984 outlived its life by 1988 and the present research 
station' 'Maitri' was made operational in 1989. Since 1981 research work is 
being carried out in the fields of Atmospheric Science, Biology and Human 
Physiology, Environmental Sciences, Earth Sciences and Glaciology, Global 
Climate Change and Engineering and Communication. 
At Maitri, eight permanent observatories have been established, which are 
providing continuous data on weather, geomagnetism, seismicity, plate 
movement, Very Low Frequency propagation, communication, 
environmental and cold acclimatization. 
So far 24 expeditions have gone to Antarctica in which more than 700 
scientists, belonging to over 50 national level institutes and organizations 
have participated. A vast array of scientific and technological information has 
been collected in addition to publicatio n of sixteen technical reports, several 
books, map and one atlas on Antarctic sea ice and more than 300 scientific 
papers. About 45 Ph. Ds have been awarded on the research work carried out 
in Antarctica.

(SHRI PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) to (d) ISRO's satellites have 
significantly contributed in facilitating development of rural and remote areas 
in various fronts. 
(i) INSAT satellites have extended television coverage to over 90% of the 
country's population. 
(ii) Telecommunication network has been extended to remote/rural areas 
through INSAT satellites by Department of Telecommunication by 
using about 370 satellite earth stations/VATs and emergency 
communications needs in remote places like Andaman & Nicobar 
Islands have been met using portable satellite communication 
terminals.

district hospitals serving rural/remote areas including Jammu &

through satellites to more than 800 primary schools in the 
predominantly tribal district of Chamarajnagar in Karnataka. 100 
satellite terminals are being used for Technical University education in 
Karnataka, 2000 terminals in school s, colleges and polytechnics in 
Andhra Pradesh, 75 terminals in Maharashtra for Open University, 25 
terminals for Technical University in Madhya Pradesh and 20 terminals 
for university education in Goa. 
(v) A study on the impact of a satellite-based developmental communication 
project conducted in Jhabua, a tribal district of Madhya Pradesh 
published in 2000 indicated benefits to the rural population in the area 
of health awareness, agricultural practices, cottage industry, fishery, 
woman and child welfare etc. About 60% of viewers reported gains in 
health awareness and about 40% reported gains in health practices. 
(vi) A study conducted in rural Karn ataka indicated a significant cost 
savings resulted from use of telemedicine connectivity via satellite. In 
general, it was observed that about 90% of the patients did not

SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: A major fire accident occurred on Mumbai 
High North (MHN) processing platform at 4.05 P.M. on 27. 7.2005 resulting in 
the loss of the facility. The accident took place when ONGC's multipurpose 
support vessel "Samudra Suraksha", under SGI operation, was engaged in a 
medicai evacuation operation. According to available information, the MSV 
lost control, drifted, and collided with the platform causing a major fire which 
also engulfed the MSV. 
Given the intensity of the fire and consequent damage the platform was 
abandoned according to a weli-rehearsed abandonment drill used in offshore 
operations, Similarly, personnel from the MSV were evacuated, except for 6 
divers who are now undergoing decompression and are expected to survive. 
Personnel on board the chartered drilling rig in NC Yester deployed in the 
area were also evacuated. The MHN platform was totally lost in less than 2 
hours along with a Pawan hans helicopter positioned on it. ONGC support 
and supply vessels and three chartered helicopters were quickly mobilized for 
search and rescue operations. Indian Navy and Coast guards provided 
prompt assistance by deploying ships and aircrafts. 
A total of 384 personnel had to abandon the affected platform and the two 
vessels. Of them, 351 have been rescued in addition to the 6 divers who are 
undergoing decompression. 
The injured persons were provided first aid by doctors and paramedics 
immediately on rescue. 129 of t hose rescued are reaching Mumbai docks 
today in the morning. The remaining rescued personnel are expected to reach 
Mumbai by last evening. The search for missing persons is continuing. 
So far, 10 personnel are confirmed dead. These include 6 from ONGC and 
1 each from the MSV and NC Yester. Two bodies are yet to be identified. On 
behalf of the nation, I extend my deepes t sympathies to be bereaved families. 
Their rehabilitation will be our duty. 
In spite of the severe destruction caused by floods and rains in Mumbai, all 
possible resources for rescue and relief were mobilized immediately.

identified more with the electronic media in India. A majority of the reputed 
international channels avoid such presentation while reporting crime and do

important that the Prasar Bharti and other concerned agencies stipulate clear 
guidelines on the content and quality of crime reporting.

the drinking water problem of both the districts.

SHRI C. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vi ce-Chairman, Sir, on behalf of my 
party, the AIADMK, I rise to put forth my views on the Citizenship 
(Amendment) Bill, 2005. This Bill is in fulfilment of the promise made by the 
hon. Prime Minister on the 'Pravasi Bhartiya Divas'. 
So far, persons of the Indian origin  belonging to only 16 nations were 
permitted to avail of this dual citizenship facility. But this Bill allows persons of 
the Indian origin from all the countr ies, except Pakistan and Bangladesh to 
avail of the dual citizenship. On the face of it, this seems to have removed the 
discrimination between nations. It is said that persons having dual citizenship 
will be entitled to come to India at will and stay as long as they desire. They 
will not be under police vigilance either. I would like to say a word of caution 
that anti-social and anti-nat ional elements can misuse this provision to come 
to India and create law and order problem. 
The authorities who process the applic ations forms for dual citizenship 
should be persons of impeccable integr ity so that undersirable persons are 
not given this facility. Once there was a serious law and order problem in 
Tamil Nadu due to the entry of anti-so cial and anti-national elements. That 
gun-culture was ended only when our respected leader Dr. Puratchi Thalaivi 
became the Chief Minister of Tamil N adu, then only Tamil Nadu became a 
garden of peace. 
I have a few points to make. Clause 7 (a) (ii) says "who is citizen of 
another country, but was a citizen of India at the time of, or at any time 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [28 July, 2005] 
after the commencement of the Constitution." I think this provision will give 
room for the misuse of discretionary power. If a person has all along been a 
citizen of another country without having been a citizen of India, it will be 
difficult to trace his antecedents. Therefore, I would like to know: who would 
decide about such person's eligibility and on what basis? 
The Bill is silent about persons of  foreign origin who became Indian 
citizens but renounced Indian- citizenship later to become a citizen of their 
own or some other nation. I would request the hon. Minister to clarify this point 
because it will not be fair to leave such  issues to the interpretation of the 
judiciary. I hope the hon. Minister woul d clarify the points raised by me. With 
these words, I conclude. Thank you.

drafted at a time when the ideal was ge nerally perceived as being that every

recognized in the international law.
